issues.legal_issue: The special succession rule for property inherited by a female intestate from her husband changes the order of succession without eliminating other classes of heirs.
material_facts: The deceased inherited the property from her husband, had no issue, and died intestate.
No heir on her husband's side was entitled to succeed.
The claimant was the grandson of the deceased's brother and claimed as an heir in another class under the general order of succession.
issues.conclusion: The special rule changes the order of succession but does not exclude the other classes of heirs altogether.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 15(1) and 15(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the special rule for property inherited from a husband gives the husband's heirs priority in the circumstances specified, but does not eliminate other classes of heirs. Section 16 Rule 3 explains how to identify heirs for the special rule, by treating the husband as having died intestate immediately after the female intestate; Section 8 and its Schedule then identify those heirs. The Court relied on Bhajya v. Gopikabai and the Joint Committee report, which described the purpose as revising the order of succession and directing property first to the husband's heirs or the source from which it came.

rule.if: female_intestate_succession_case and inherited_property_from_husband and no_issue and husband_side_heirs_absent and other_general_order_heir_exists

predicates.female_intestate_succession_case: The dispute concerns succession to the estate of a female who died intestate.
predicates.inherited_property_from_husband: The female intestate had inherited the disputed property from her husband.
predicates.no_issue: The female intestate left no son or daughter, including descendants who would take their place.
predicates.husband_side_heirs_absent: No heir of the husband was entitled to succeed to the property.
predicates.other_general_order_heir_exists: A person belonging to another class in the general order of succession was an heir of the female intestate.

issues.definition: When a female intestate inherited property from her husband, left no issue, and no heir on her husband's side is entitled to succeed, the existence of another heir in the general order means that the other class remains eligible rather than being excluded altogether.

issues.legal_issue: The State takes an intestate's property by escheat only when there is a total absence of heirs qualified to succeed.
material_facts: The deceased died intestate and had inherited the property from her husband.
There was no heir on her husband's side entitled to succeed.
The claimant asserted a right to inherit as an heir in another class under the general order of succession.
The State claimed the property on the basis that there had been a failure of heirs.
issues.conclusion: The State was not entitled to the property by escheat because the existence of an heir under either succession order prevents escheat.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies only on a failure of heirs, meaning the total absence of heirs qualified to succeed; the State takes subject to the property's obligations and liabilities and is not a rival or preferential heir. Read with Sections 15 and 16, the property of a female intestate cannot escheat if she leaves an heir under either Section 15(1) or Section 15(2). The Court also referred to Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th ed., volume 17, paragraph 1439, on escheat to the Crown as lord paramount.

predicates.intestate_escheat_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim that an intestate's estate passes to the State because of a failure of heirs.
predicates.heir_under_general_order_exists: At least one person is qualified to inherit under the general order of succession applicable to the intestate.
predicates.heir_under_special_order_exists: At least one person is qualified to inherit under a special order of succession applicable to the property.

issues.definition: In an intestate escheat dispute, the existence of an heir under either applicable succession order means the estate does not pass to the State by escheat.

issues.legal_issue: A decree for possession against mortgagees cannot stand when the claimant's right to redeem the mortgage was expressly left undecided by agreement at trial.
material_facts: The claimant sought possession of the property and a declaration that he could redeem property held by mortgagees.
At trial, the question whether the mortgage subsisted was expressly left open by agreement between counsel.
The High Court later decreed possession against the mortgagees without that question having been adjudicated.
issues.conclusion: The decree against the mortgagees was set aside, the suit against them was dismissed, and the parties could adjudicate the subsistence of the mortgage elsewhere.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the decree against the mortgagees was untenable because the claimant's right to redeem and the subsistence of the mortgage had not been adjudicated and had expressly been left open by agreement. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_against_possession_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree for possession against persons holding property as mortgagees.
predicates.redemption_issue_left_open_by_agreement: The parties agreed that the claimant's right to redeem the mortgage would be left undecided at trial.
predicates.mortgage_subsistence_not_adjudicated: The trial court did not decide whether the mortgage continued to subsist.

issues.definition: In an appeal against a possession decree, if the parties agreed to leave redemption unresolved and the mortgage's subsistence was not adjudicated, the decree against the mortgagees is set aside.
